item.title: Water Meter Running When No Water Is Being Used: Causes and Fixes
item.description:
Quick Answer

# Water Meter Running When No Water Is Being Used: Causes and Fixes

If your water meter is running when no water is used, you almost certainly have a leak somewhere in your plumbing system, or your meter is malfunctioning due to air pressure or debris. This is a critical warning sign that you are paying for water you aren't actually using, which can lead to significantly higher utility bills and potential property damage. While minor movement might be caused by air in the lines or pressure spikes from the municipal supply, continuous spinning indicates a loss of water that requires immediate investigation.

item.title: Water Meter Leak Indicator Explained: How to Tell If Water Is Running When Everything
item.description:
The problem: your bill jumped, but you cannot see where the water went

A higher water bill is one of the most confusing household surprises. You did not change your routine... but your usage did.

When that happens, the fastest way to get clarity is to stop guessing and use your meter. Many water meters have a small "leak indicator" designed for exactly this.

This article shows you how to find the indicator, how to test correctly, and how to avoid common false alarms.

item.title: How to Read a Water Meter (and Know If Its Accurate)
item.description:
Know your meter type first

Most homes have either a dial meter or a digital meter. Dial meters use a series of small dials and a sweep hand. Digital meters show numbers directly and often include a leak indicator icon. The unit of measure is usually gallons or cubic feet. Your bill should state which unit your utility uses.

If you see cubic feet, remember that one cubic foot equals 7.48 gallons. Some bills list usage in hundred cubic feet (CCF). That is 100 cubic feet, or 748 gallons.

item.title: Is Your Toilet Running? A Simple Leak Test (and How It Shows Up on Your Water Bill)
item.description:
Why a running toilet is hard to notice (but shows up on the bill)

A running toilet is one of the most frustrating utility problems: it can waste a lot of water without looking "broken."

Sometimes you hear the toilet refill randomly. Sometimes you hear nothing at all. But your water meter keeps counting, and your bill is where the problem finally shows up.

If you're trying to understand the full water-bill structure, start with Water Service Explained. If you're in "why did this spike?" mode, see why water bills suddenly increase .

item.title: What Is CCF on a Water Bill? (Cubic Feet Explained in Plain English)
item.description:
Start here: what CCF means on a water bill

If you opened your water bill and saw "CCF," you are not alone. It is one of those utility terms that feels obvious to the utility and totally unclear to everyone else.

Here is the simple definition: CCF means "hundred cubic feet." It is a unit of volume--how much water flowed through your meter during the billing period.

This article gives you a plain-English conversion you can trust, plus a quick way to connect the CCF number to what you actually pay.
